thread:
mike: uploaded an nsys trace and perfetto capture for the client-reported perf regression. high-level: HBM bandwidth has sharp spikes correlating with KV cache walk storms when we hit long sequences (>2048). link: https://perfetto.example/redwood/trace/1917004321 :eyes:

anita: saw the trace, quick q — do we have the kernel selection timeline overlaid? want to see when we fall back to the slower matmul path. also please paste the nsys command you used.

mike: nsys cmd I used: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn --output=run_1917004321 python server_trace.py --scenario longseq-mix`\. Attached the perfetto link and the raw nvvp (s3://redwood-traces/1917004321.nvvp).

yuan: brief initial read: looks like two things colliding: 1) our kernel selector decides to switch kernels once the runtime predicts >3k tokens in-flight for a request shape; that alternative kernel has worse memory coalescing so HBM reads balloon. 2) batching heuristics create microbatch groups that mix short + very long sequences, producing a KV readstorm as the long seqs repeatedly probe KV pages.

luis: can you paste the small nvprof-like summary? even top-5 kernels with %time and DRAM read/write would help.

mike: pasted a short extract from the nsys report: `Top kernels: matmul_fused 42% (DRAM read 120 GB), matmul_v2 31% (DRAM read 480 GB), kv_load_paged 9% (DRAM read 330 GB)`. HBM peak read ~520 GB/s (from hw counters), sustained ~410 GB/s for bursts ~120ms. tail lat spikes on kv_load_paged up to 180ms.

anita: that matmul_v2 DRAM number looks suspect — it implies poor tiling for wide heads. interesting it's chosen only for long inputs. does the selector use sequence-length only or also estimated kv-hit-rate?

yuan: selector currently uses sequence length + estimated tokens-in-flight from batcher; it does NOT incorporate kv-hit-rate. if you have lots of cold KV pages (long seqs probing many history pages), the memory pattern becomes pointer-chasing and kills locality. we should add a cheap kv-hit-rate estimator into the decision.

perfetto-bot: perfetto: flamegraph + GPU slices uploaded -> https://perfetto.example/redwood/flame/1917004321

mike: re-ran a controlled reproduce with synthetic workload: seq distribution [64x20%, 512x50%, 4096x30%], 8-concurrent requests, batcher config: max_tokens=65536, window=12. result: same HBM spikes, and end-to-end p95 increases by ~3.4x vs baseline (all-512).

luis: quick mitigation idea: change batcher to avoid mixing extreme long seqs with short ones (micro-scheduling by seqlen buckets). also consider KV prefetching for long seqs to spread reads early.

anita: yes, bucketed batching is low-risk. but prefetch might increase peak bandwidth unless we spread it out over the request timeline. we should test both.

yuan: reproduced locally with a smaller GPU set. small experiment results: disabling kv-prefetch dropped HBM peak by ~22% and tail lat by ~35%, but overall throughput dipped ~12% because more stalls while waiting for on-demand KV loads.

mike: posted the perfetto timeline highlighting when the kernel switch happens and the KV readburst windows (see arrows). :point_up: those readstorms line up exactly with matmul_v2 slices.

luis: question — is the kernel switch heuristic using sequence length threshold 2048? I recall a recent commit bumped that to 3072 for some models.

yuan: commit 9f3b changed thresholds for gpt-like shapes; current live uses 3072. in this trace though the selector flipped at ~3500 estimated tokens-in-flight due to aggressive batching aggregation. so both the threshold and the batcher grouping contributed.

anita: plan proposal: 1) short-term: patch batcher to avoid mixing seqlen>2.5k with <=512 in same microbatch; 2) medium: add kv-hit-rate estimator to kernel selector; 3) long-term: consider kernel improvement to reduce DRAM pressure for the fallback path.

mike: +1 to 1 and 2. I can prototype a batcher switch that enforces per-microbatch seqlen bucket. will run sweep.

luis: I'll run hardware sweep on 8xA100 and 4xA800 to see hardware sensitivity (HBM bandwidth differences). posting results to this thread.

yuan: pseudo patch for selector addition (very rough):
```
if estimated_tokens_in_flight > K and kv_estimated_miss_rate > 0.4:
    choose_kernel = low_dram_kernel
else:
    choose_kernel = fast_kernel
```
we need a cheap kv_estimator: sample one request per batch and count unique page touches over the last N tokens. cheap approximate counters should work.

anita: agree. also add NVTX ranges around batching decisions so we can directly map batcher choices -> kernel switches in traces. include those in the next nsys run.

mike: quick repro command for the team: `python tools/run_perf_sweep.py --model gpt-13b --seq-mix 64,512,4096 --clients 8 --nsys --nvtx --out s3://redwood-traces/191700_repro/`

perfetto-bot: uploaded perfetto + trace view for the bucketed-batching experiment -> https://perfetto.example/redwood/flame/191700_bucketed

luis: initial bucketed-batching run: HBM peak down 18%, p95 down ~28%, throughput -4% (acceptable trade). will run more seeds. :thumbsup:

yuan: will start a bench branch with kv-estimator and also add a lightweight metric that surfaces per-request kv_page_touch_rate in the console so we can correlate.

anita: assigning follow-ups: @mike prototype batcher switch, @luis hardware sweeps, @yuan selector changes + console metric. we'll reconvene after sweep results.

mike: noted, starting on the batcher prototype now. will drop a short PR with microbench results.

luis: uploading initial sweep logs to s3://redwood-bench/191700_hw_sweep.tar.gz

mike: thanks everyone. if you need the raw traces ping me and I can share nvvp.

anita: nice root-cause triangulation. keeping this thread pinned until we have the PRs and perf numbers. :white_check_mark: 

perfetto-bot: reminder: traces auto-expire in 30d unless archived.
